common_name: Orange Glow Seaberry (Eastern European Sea Buckthorn)

planting.note: This is a female clone, so plant one male seaberry for every 6-8 females to ensure wind pollination.

directions: Orange Glow is an Eastern European sea buckthorn selection grown for its heavy crop of large, vivid yellow-orange berries with a sharp citrus-and-guava flavor, popular in preserves and beverages. Like other sea buckthorns, it is thorny enough to serve as an informal hedge and fixes nitrogen in the soil, benefiting neighboring plants. Because it relies on wind rather than insects for pollination, a male plant must be sited nearby, and no special vernalization is needed for the plant to set fruit, typically ready for harvest around August in Pacific Northwest conditions.

planting.note: Plant a grafted or cutting-grown tree in full to half-day sun in well-drained soil; this Florida-origin selection is one of the more heat- and humidity-tolerant mulberries One Green World carries.

directions: Lakeland Tropical was selected in Florida and bears dark, blackberry-like fruit on a vigorous tree with glossy, tropical-looking foliage, reportedly cropping as heavily as Illinois Everbearing even in the Pacific Northwest. Give it full to half-day sun and well-drained soil; it is self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, typically starting 2-3 years after planting. Harvest from midsummer into early fall and use the berries fresh or dried, since the tree is largely untroubled by pests or disease once established.

planting.note: Plant in full to half-day sun in well-drained soil; this Korean cultivar stays relatively compact compared to standard mulberry trees, making it a better fit for smaller home orchards.

directions: Ik Soo Bong is a Korean mulberry selection prized for large, juicy, nearly black fruit produced in heavy, extended flushes from midsummer into early fall. It stays somewhat more compact than many mulberry trees, reaching 12-15 feet, which makes it easier to net or hand-harvest. The tree is self-fertile and needs no pollinator partner, and it shows good natural resistance to the pests and diseases that sometimes trouble mulberries elsewhere.

planting.note: Plant in full to half-day sun in well-drained soil; Grover's Best ripens earlier than Illinois Everbearing, so pairing the two extends the harvest window considerably.

directions: Grover's Best produces unusually large, sweet-tart mulberries and ripens ahead of Illinois Everbearing, giving growers an earlier start to mulberry season. The tree develops dark green, tropical-looking foliage and reaches 15-20 feet or more at maturity, so give it room and full to half-day sun. It is self-fertile and reliably productive, typically bearing within 2-3 years of planting, with fruit best used fresh or dried for winter snacking.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained soil; Black Topaz is a large-fruited selection of the fragrant-flowered clove currant, tougher and more drought-tolerant than European black currants.

directions: Black Topaz is a clove currant selected for notably large, jet-black berries that follow a spring flush of fragrant yellow, clove-scented flowers. Plant in full to half-day sun in well-drained soil; it is self-fertile and begins bearing within 1-2 years, ripening in July. Because it tolerates heat and drought better than Ribes nigrum types, it works well as a dual-purpose ornamental hedge as well as a fruit crop, needing only light removal of old wood each winter.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Delindmoi is a French black currant selection valued for strong powdery mildew resistance.

directions: Delindmoi is a French-bred black currant that sets heavy crops of deep black, aromatic berries from a young age and holds up better against powdery mildew than many older European selections. Grow it in fertile, well-drained soil in full to half-day sun, mulching to protect its shallow roots. It is self-fertile and bears within 1-2 years of planting, ripening in July; the fruit dries well for winter storage in addition to fresh eating, juicing, and baking.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Black Reward is a late-flowering Dutch selection, which helps it dodge spring frosts that can damage earlier-blooming currants.

directions: Black Reward is a Dutch midseason black currant noted among growers for exceptionally rich flavor, with berry size varying within each cluster but yields running consistently heavy. Its comparatively late bloom time helps crops escape late frosts that can wipe out earlier currant varieties. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full to half-day sun; it is self-fertile, bears within 1-2 years, and ripens in July, suiting fresh eating, juicing, and baking.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in moderately fertile, well-drained soil; Jewel is a Polish selection valued for unusual peach-colored fruit and strong powdery mildew resistance.

directions: Jewel is a Polish gooseberry selection that stands out for its large, peach-colored berries, a less common color break from the usual green or red gooseberry types. The compact 2-3 foot shrub is self-fertile, disease-resistant, and begins fruiting within 1-2 years, ripening in July for fresh eating, pies, and preserves. Grow it in full to half-day sun in well-drained soil, and simply watch for currant worms, which can be removed by hand if they appear on the foliage.

common_name: Red George Gooseberry (Ukrainian Dark Red Gooseberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained soil; Red George is a Ukrainian selection bred for very dark red fruit and strong powdery mildew resistance.

directions: Red George is a Ukrainian gooseberry bred for abundant crops of striking, nearly black-red berries with a sweet flavor that holds up well for fresh eating. The compact, 2-3 foot bush is self-fertile, cold-hardy to -40 degrees F, and shows good resistance to powdery mildew, a common gooseberry problem. Site it in full to half-day sun in well-drained soil, and watch for currant worms on the foliage, which can simply be picked off by hand.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in moderately fertile, well-drained soil; Selby is a Canadian-bred, disease-resistant gooseberry that can bear fruit in its very first year.

directions: Selby is a Canadian gooseberry forming an upright, attractive shrub that can begin fruiting the same year it's planted, with sweet, large purple-red berries following in June and July. It is self-fertile, shade-tolerant, and cold-hardy to -40 degrees F, making it a reliable choice for colder gardens. Grow in full to partial sun in moderately fertile, well-drained soil, and prune out canes older than four years to keep harvests strong.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in moderately fertile, well-drained soil; Siewka K1 is a Polish selection that needs at least 1,000 chill hours, so it is best suited to regions with real winter cold.

directions: Siewka K1 is a Polish gooseberry forming a compact, 2-3 foot shrub loaded with abundant, sweet, purplish-red berries that ripen in June and July. It is self-fertile, disease-resistant, and can begin fruiting as early as its planting year, making it a quick-payoff choice for new plantings. Give it full to partial sun in moderately fertile, well-drained soil; because it requires over 1,000 chill hours, it performs best in climates with a real winter rather than mild southern regions.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained soil, and pair with another late-blooming honeyberry variety with matching bloom time for cross-pollination.

directions: Taka is a late-blooming honeyberry that flowers roughly two months after early types in the Pacific Northwest, which lines its bloom up with peak pollinator activity and improves fruit set. The upright bush produces large, sweet, blue-skinned berries in May and June that cling well to the plant instead of dropping early, easing harvest. It is cold-hardy to about -35 degrees F but, like all honeyberries, needs a second late-blooming variety nearby for cross-pollination; grow it in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in moderately fertile, well-drained soil, and plant alongside a similarly timed variety such as Borealis for pollination.

directions: Strawberry Sensation is a honeyberry bred by Lidia R. Delafield Stuart with a distinctive sweet-tart flavor carrying a noticeable alpine-strawberry aftertaste behind the usual blueberry-like honeyberry taste. The upright, densely branched shrub grows 4-6 feet tall and ripens its blue berries in May and June, among the earliest fruit of the garden season. It needs a second variety with a matching bloom time, such as Borealis, for cross-pollination, and performs best in full to partial sun in moderately fertile, well-drained soil, tolerating winter cold down to roughly zone 2.

planting.note: Direct sow cold-moist stratified seed into consistently moist to wet soil along a shaded path or woodland edge, since this clumping sedge naturalizes readily in damp shade.

directions: Wood Gray Sedge is a tidy, clump-forming woodland sedge native to wet forests and shaded roadside ditches across the eastern United States. Despite the common name it reads more deep green than gray, with slender hairless blades that hold their color through the growing season. It thrives in the dappled light and damp humus of a streamside or low woodland garden where many turf grasses fail, needing little care beyond consistent moisture once established. Use it as a textural filler beneath shrubs or along a shaded drainage swale.
